div.head: Many LAN (Local Area Network) protocols that "solve" the problem of achieving real-time communications have been published. However they have been traditionally examined under assumptions that are not usually met with distributed systems. In this paper, the class of on-line protocols which exhibit deterministic properties in spite of lack of global knowledge are considered. Such protocols (e.g. tree protocols) yield computable bounds on the duration of collision resolution. This paper shows that combining such deterministic properties with feasibilio tests, as those developed in realtime scheduling, permits to design provably correct hard real-time protocols.
div.p: First we extend a centralized real-time problem to a decentralized context using the idea of extra cost. Second the applicability of our results is then illustrated with the CSMA-DCR (Ethernet with deterministic collision resolution) protocol, which is currently used in real settings.

div.head: 1: Introduction
div.p: Designing Real-Time distributed systems requires communication protocols specifically developed to satisfy timing constraints requirements. One of the most common constraint is known as deadline satisfaction.

Classical approaches in Real-Time local area networks concerned with the MAC level of the OS1 model consist in considering that traffic pattems generated by all the components of the system are well known before design. Therefore, a static method (TDMA, polling) is used to share the channel in order to satisfy the prescribed deadlines.

Such methods lead to many practical problems such as difficulty of chosing the parameters, largely overdimensioned bandwidth, difficulty in proving that assumptions will not be violated in the future, and lack of flexibility. Especially, what is obvious to whom is familiar with distributed problems, these methods contradict the hypothesis that transmission delays are not exactly known a priori, neither the arrival times, or times when stations are allowed to transmit. Consequently design of real-time distributed systems can only rest on a partial knowledge of the future [6].

The other approaches, the on-line ones, consist in being able to make a decision at any time during the system lifetime without a priori knowledge of future arrivals. Some on-line algorithms exhibit a very interesting property for real-time transmission: determinism behavior. Such a property will be shown to be useful to solve, on-line, the problem of transmitting real-time messages, and to define feasibility conditions for sets of messages. One originality of this work is to treat a networking problem as a scheduling problem. We show the applicability of the results with a real example.

Notice that solving a problem with an off-line algorithm leads to solve this particular problem only. Modification of any initial parameter invalidates the solution. On the other hand, solving a problem with an on-line algorithm can lead to solve a general problem, and to prove the feasibility of a many sets of messages, including the particular cases solved by off-line algorithms. That is why we use an online approach combined with proven properties to solve the problem of real-time communications.

div.head: 2: A brief survey of previous work
div.p: As stated before this paper deals with the problem according to the dual approach of scheduling and real-time network access.

In the domain of scheduling most of centralized realtime scheduling algorithms that have been studied are statical priority driven algorithms. When the system starts all the parameters needed to compute the priority of all the tasks are supposed known. Each task priority is computed and definitively assigned to it. Then, at any time, the task with the highest priority, among all the tasks released, is executed.
A scheduling algorithm that allows tasks to be interrupted and resumed later is said to be preemptive. Otherwise it is non-preemptive.

When preemption of tasks is allowed, Liu and Layland [3] proposed an optimal on-line scheduling algorithm called EDF (Earliest Deadline First). They also indicate a necessary and sufficient condition of schedulability of a set of periodic tasks.

When preemption is not allowed the problem becomes much more difficult. Without additional constraints no priority driven scheduling is optimal for an arbitrary nonpreemptive system [4]. However, with the non-idling constraint (see section 3), Jeffay, Stanat and Martel [l] have developed a necessary and sufficient condition for a non-preemptive periodic tasks set to be schedulable and shown that in this case EDF is optimal.
In the network domain a very common MAC protocol is Ethemet, also known as IS0 8802.3 [13][141. Its more important properties are:

decentralized, each station uses the same local algorithm. No other global knowledge than the channel status is necessary to take a decision, easy to implement at low cost, robustness under transient faults [7],
flexibility, and fast response time at low level traffic load.

Yet, it has a great drawback for use in real-time applications because it uses a probabilistic retransmission policy called the Binary Exponential Backoff that causes unbounded transmission delays and breaks down at heavy load.

A way to stabilize the protocol is to replace BEB retransmission policy by a tree algorithm. This has been shown efficient for group testing and multiple access problems [91[10][11][121. Furthermore, tree algorithm is easy to implement in a decentralized and deterministic way. Such a protocol has been developed and patented [8]. Various options of it are currently implemented in industrial products such as the FACTOR factory LAN from CAP-APTOR, the Recital VME board from Dassault Electronique, the 82596 Ethemet chip from INTEL.

The 802.3D protocol, also known as CSMA-DCR for Deterministic Collision Resolution, is based on 802.3 protocol. The only difference leads on the internal collision resolution mechanism: 802.3 uses the instable Binary Exponential Backoff algorithm while CSMA-DCR uses a stable and deterministic binary tree algorithm.

While no collision occurs, CSMA-DCR behaves exactly like Ethemet. Upon collision occurrence, a resolution "epoch" starts based, for each station, on the following knowledge: feedback information provided by the channel (idle, busy or collided), a local counter and a unique index. The tree algorithm, according to the channel status and the unique index, schedules the transmissions so that, with certainty, each of the conflicting stations eventually succeeds to transmit.
Deterministic behavior is a consequence of the bounded duration of an epoch. Let us show now that this property can be used to obtain hard real-time protocol.

By definition a message set is said to be schedulable if it exists a feasible schedule according to which all requests of all messages can be processed to meet their respective deadlines. Moreover a scheduling algorithm is said to be optimal if it will constructs a feasible schedule for every schedulable set of hard real time messages [3].

According to our Hard real time aim, each message invocation results in its successful transmission at a time specified by the combination of both: a local scheduling algorithm. a decentralized access channel algorithm. This paper deals in the sequel with a specific hard realtime distributed scheduling problem. l k o efficient algorithms are combined in order to mix their natural properties (reliability, flexibility, determinism ...) with feasibility conditions adapted to various hard real-time traffics. The main characteristic of our context is the extra-cost to pay for coping with the decentralized access channel algorithm due to the lack of global knowledge. In this paper we focus on this problem.
In the two following sections a set of sufficient, i.e. pessimistic ones, conditions on the durations and periods of messages are given for a message set to be schedulable.

The extra-cost of making online decisions is the price to pay for not having a priori knowledge of the release times of messages. This cost could be greatly reduced if release times were known, but this could be an unrealistic constraint for a real application.

Optimality and competitive ratio of the CSMA-DCR protocol would be very useful figures. Two other interesting developments are: (a) the extension of the results in the case where the deadlines of messages could be different from the instant of the next arrival of that message, PioDi, and (b) the behavior of these protocols in overloaded cases or with aperiodic traffics. These problems are currently under study within Project REFLECS, INRIA.
